title: Tale of the Trader and the Jinn

keywords: tale of the trader and the jinn
full_text:
There was once a prosperous merchant of Baghdad who possessed great wealth, vast estates, and an unblemished reputation for honesty. One summer, having debts to collect in a distant province, he mounted his horse, filled his saddlebags with dried dates, biscuits, and a flask of cool water, and set forth across the dusty plains.

Having accomplished his business successfully, he turned homeward. On the fourth day, beneath the blazing midday sun, he sought refuge under the spreading boughs of a wild walnut tree near a bubbling spring. He tethered his steed, opened his wallet, and began to eat sweet dates, tossing the hard stones casually across his shoulder. Suddenly, the earth trembled. A dense column of smoke billowed from the sand, twisting into the towering form of an enormous Jinni, whose eyes glowed like coals and who brandished a naked scimitar of blue steel.

"Arise, O wretched mortal!" roared the spirit in a voice of thunder. "I must slay you even as you have slain my son!" The merchant trembled with amazement and cried: "How could a frail creature like me slay a child of the unseen?" The Jinni answered wrathfully: "When you cast away your date stones without warning, one struck my invisible son in the breast, and he expired on the instant. Blood demands blood!"

The merchant fell upon his knees and wept bitterly: "I had no malice, O mighty spirit! Spare my life, for I have a loving wife, young children, and debts of honor yet unpaid." Seeing the Jinni unmoved, the merchant made a noble plea: "Grant me a reprieve of one single year. By the Creator of the heavens, I swear to return to this very tree on the anniversary of this day, that you may execute your judgment upon me. Let me but divide my inheritance, provide for my family, and discharge every coin I owe to my creditors."

The Jinni, astonished by the man's solemn oath and steadfast character, bound him to the covenant and vanished into the earth. The merchant returned home, fulfilled all his obligations, embraced his weeping family with tearful farewells, and when the year drew to its close, put on his shroud and rode back to the walnut tree, choosing death with honor over life bought by broken faith.
moral: Honesty and keeping one's sacred word in the face of death inspire mercy and invoke the highest virtues in others.

Believing rumors and flattery without proof
